{{Short description|Statistical method for handling missing data}}
[[File:Listwise-deletion-example.png|thumb|right|A visual example of list wise deletion]]
In [[statistics]], '''listwise deletion''' is a method for handling [[missing data]]. In this method, an entire record is excluded from analysis if any single value is missing.<ref name="Allison2001">{{cite book |last=Allison |first=P. D. |year=2001 |title=Missing Data |series=Sage University Papers Series on Quantitative Applications in the Social Sciences |volume=07-136 |location=Thousand Oaks, CA |publisher=Sage }}</ref>{{rp|6}}

==Example==
For example, consider the following questionnaire, as answered by 10 subjects:

|-

A researcher is hoping to [[Statistical model|model]] income ([[Dependent and independent variables|dependent variable]]) based on age and gender (independent variables). Using listwise deletion, the researcher would remove subjects 3, 4, and 8 from the [[Sample (statistics)|sample]] before performing any further analysis.

==Problems with listwise deletion==
Listwise deletion affects [[statistical power]] of the tests conducted.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Roth |first=P. L. |year=1994 |title=Missing data: A conceptual review for applied psychologists |journal=Personnel Psychology |volume=47 |issue=3 |pages=537–559 |doi=10.1111/j.1744-6570.1994.tb01736.x }}</ref><ref name="Olinsky et al., 2003">{{cite journal |last=Olinsky |first=A. |last2=Chen |first2=S. |last3=Harlow |first3=L. |year=2003 |title=The comparative efficacy of imputations methods for missing data in structural equation modeling |journal=European Journal of Operational Research |volume=151 |issue=1 |pages=53–79 |doi=10.1016/S0377-2217(02)00578-7 }}</ref> Statistical power relies in part on high sample size. Because listwise deletion excludes data with missing values, it reduces the sample which is being statistically analysed.

Listwise deletion is also problematic when the reason for missing data [[Missing data#Missing not at random|may not be random]] (i.e., questions in [[Questionnaire|questionnaires]] aiming to extract sensitive information.<ref name="Olinsky et al., 2003" /> Due to the method, much of the subjects' data will be excluded from analysis, leaving a [[Bias (statistics)|bias]] in data findings. For instance, a questionnaire may include questions about respondents drug use history, current earnings, or sexual persuasions. Many of the subjects in the sample may not answer due to the intrusive nature of the questions, but may answer all other items. Listwise deletion will exclude these respondents from analysis. This may create a bias as participants who do divulge this information may have different characteristics than participants who do not. [[Multiple imputation]] is an alternate technique for dealing with missing data that attempts to eliminate this bias.

==Compared to other methods==
While listwise deletion does have its problems, it is preferable to many other methods for handling missing data.<ref name="Allison2001" />{{rp|7}} In some cases, it may even be the least problematic method.<ref name="Allison2001" />{{rp|6}}  The following table provides some comparisons of listwise deletions to other methods:

|-
! Method
! Comparison
|-
| [[Pairwise deletion]]
| Ambiguous definition of sample size causes bias in estimated [[Standard error|standard errors]] and test statistics.<ref name="Allison2001" />{{rp|9}}
|-

| Produces biased estimates of coefficients.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Jones |first=M. P. |year=1996 |title=Indicator and stratification methods for missing explanatory variables in multiple linear regression |journal=[[Journal of the American Statistical Association|J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.]] |volume=91 |issue=433 |pages=222–230 |doi=10.1080/01621459.1996.10476680 }} As cited by Allison (2001), p. 10.</ref>
